title: Kondo Lattice model for field induced triplet pairing in CeRh$_2$As$_2$
abstract: Spin triplet superconductors are of interest because of their topological properties, and their robustness to high magnetic fields. CeRh$_2$As$_2$ is a unique heavy fermion superconductor with both even-parity and candidate odd-parity superconducting phases with a special feature enabling a field induced phase transition between the two. The field induced transition which switches the parity of the Cooper pairs is enabled by a staggered antisymmetric spin orbit coupling (ASOC) interaction. However, the heavy fermion origins of the superconductivity in CeRh$_2$As$_2$ and the origin of the antisymmetric spin-orbit coupling are currently unexplored. Here, we develop a Kondo lattice model for CeRh$_2$As$_2$ and demonstrate how local hybridization between Cerium $d$- and $f$-orbitals, driven by the locally broken inversion symmetry, at the Cerium sites generates the ASOC. The resulting Kondo lattice model leads to nearly degenerate even and odd parity superconducting states that display a field induced parity transition between an even-parity state and an odd-parity pseudospin triplet state. We discuss the wider implications of our results extended to other heavy fermion systems like CeSiI.
summary: This theoretical work models superconductivity in CeRh2As2 using a Kondo lattice approach to explain the field-induced transition between even and odd parity superconducting states. The key finding is that local symmetry breaking generates an Anti-Symmetric SOC, which stabilizes these competing pairing symmetries. It provides a general framework for understanding unconventional pairing in heavy fermion systems.
main_problem: The paper addresses the origin of superconductivity in the heavy fermion superconductor CeRh2As2, specifically focusing on the mechanism behind the field-induced phase transition between even and odd parity superconducting states.
main_result: The authors develop a Kondo lattice model showing that local hybridization driven by broken inversion symmetry generates an Anti-Symmetric SOC (ASOC), leading to nearly degenerate even and odd parity superconducting states and predicting a field-induced parity transition.
method: The methodology involves developing a Kondo lattice model, calculating the f-electron self-energy, and using group theory (symplectic group) to analyze the symmetry constraints on the pairing states.
model_or_system: The system is CeRh2As2, a heavy fermion superconductor. The model is a Kondo lattice Hamiltonian incorporating local hybridization terms that break inversion symmetry, leading to the ASOC interaction.
key_observables: Field-driven parity transition between even-parity and odd-parity pseudospin triplet superconducting states; symmetry-allowed pairing states (Table I).
important_parameters: Magnetic field (near 4 T); hybridization strength (W); Kondo coupling strength (J).
main_assumptions: The analysis uses a mean-field approach, approximates the conduction electrons with a single band, and assumes the ASOC arises from local parity breaking hybridization.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the crystal structure and shows two pairing possibilities stabilized by staggered ASOC (uniform vs. staggered solutions).
paper_structure: The paper develops the Kondo lattice model, derives the ASOC term from local hybridization, analyzes the resulting competing even/odd parity superconducting states, and discusses implications for other heavy fermion systems.
why_interesting: The mechanism of generating unconventional pairing symmetries (like odd-parity pairing) via structural symmetry breaking (local inversion symmetry breaking) is a general theme in strongly correlated materials, relevant to understanding pairing in non-centrosymmetric superconductors.

These are the Ce(A) and Ce(B) which are related to one another by in- version. There is the electric potential coming from the Rh atoms depicted by green arrows. Right: the two pairing pos- sibilities stabilized by staggered ASOC interaction. The ∆α0 is the uniform solution which has the same sign pairing gap and ∆α3 is the staggered solution which has a modulated pairing gap on alternating layers. FIG. 2. The depiction of orbitals overlapping on an atom. In green and blue is the p-orbital which has a node and in purple is the isotropic s-orbital a.) Left: inversion center is located at the atomic center which has an even atomic potential V (x) = V (−x). The spatial overlap integral between p and s orbitals is zero, W = 0 due to the atomic potential is even. Right: orbitals have well defined parity, b.) Inversion is broken at the atomic sites, the local crystal fields distort the orbitals leading to an offset of the inversion center. The atomic potential is no longer even V (x) ̸= V (−x). The resulting overlap integral between p and s orbitals is finite W ̸= 0.

FIG. 3. The normal state bandstructure plotted along the high symmetry points. The intralayer hopping is given by t = 5, the interlayer hopping ts = 1.5 and the f electron hopping is tf = 0.5, the chemical potential µ = −1 and the f electron constraint λ = −1.7, the hybridization strengths are V = 3 and W = 2. The doubly degenerate bands are ensured by Kramer’s degeneracy.

FIG. 5. The superconducting phase diagram of applied field Bz along the z-axis w.r.t T for uniform ∆kα0 and staggered ∆kα3 phases. The SC1 phase is given by the uniform state which is Pauli limited and the high field SC2 phase is given by the staggered state. The Tc was calculated by computing the pair susceptibility χP (Bz, Tc) obtained from taking the second derivative w.r.t pairing field ∆. The first order phase transition line is shown in purple which separates the two second order phase transitions.
